Emma Tucker
 
Two U.S. Foes Join Forces—and Threaten to Further Destabilize the Middle East
 
Plus, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigns after months of tension with Pete Hegseth, and why Seattle and D.C. are drawing more families with kids
 
 
AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Two implacable U.S. foes have locked into an unlikely marriage of convenience. Yemen’s Houthi rebels and al-Shabaab—al Qaeda’s wealthiest affiliate—were long divided by sectarian lines. But shared hatred of the West and a trade of weapons, training and cash have brought them together.

 

Michael M. Phillips explains how a single broker helped set this alliance in motion before a U.S. airstrike killed him. His legacy is a dangerous partnership that threatens a strategic maritime chokepoint for the global oil trade and risks further destabilizing the Middle East.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned following months of tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

 

• Mine warfare with Iran is hampering U.S. efforts to win control over the Strait of Hormuz.

 

• Ukraine’s growing ability to strike deep inside Russia is thanks to long-range drones such as the Mammoth, which can fly 1,500 miles.

 

• A last-minute bid by California Gov. Gavin Newsom to reduce electric utilities’ wildfire liabilities failed in the state legislature after an outcry from survivors.

 

• A former Crips gang leader was convicted of murder for orchestrating the drive-by killing ‌of hip-hop legend Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas three decades ago.

 

• The FTC sued Amazon, alleging the e-commerce giant deceived advertisers by secretly raising the minimum price they had to pay to place ads promoting their products. Here’s how the FTC says the practice worked.

• The SEC has stepped up its examinations of firms behind so-called special purpose vehicles that purport to offer exposure to private company investments.

 

• Anthropic has signed a cloud-computing deal worth $35 billion with Nvidia-backed cloud provider Lambda, with Nvidia itself holding the lease on the data center.

 

• Jersey Mike’s is winning the sandwich war. But it still needs to win over Gen Z, writes David Wainer.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

A Brazilian billionaire helped shape Trump’s beef import plan.

 

Rising beef prices have been a vexing conundrum for the Trump administration. The president’s decision to temporarily waive tariffs on foreign beef was meant to cool grocery bills—but it infuriated American farmers, ranchers and the Republicans fighting for their votes in coming midterms. The day before the announcement, Brazilian billionaire Joesley Batista—who shares control of JBS, the world’s largest meatpacker—lobbied President Trump to lower the import tax. It isn’t the first time JBS has helped to shape the administration’s views, report Patrick Thomas, Natalie Andrews and Brian Schwartz. The company is among four major meatpackers under Justice Department investigation over possible anticompetitive behavior. The companies have denied any wrongdoing.

 

5.

 

Seattle and D.C. are bucking the trend by attracting families with kids.

 

Most big, expensive cities are seeing a fall in child numbers as families struggle to cover the cost of living. The opposite is happening in Seattle and Washington, D.C., two pricey coastal cities diverging from the broader demographic trajectory. The number of kids rose 10% in both places, even as it fell in most other similar cities. Seattle and D.C. have vast differences, but possess a few common ingredients that seem to have spurred their growing population of children: high-paying jobs and decent local schools, report Rachel Louise Ensign and Paul Overberg.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Watch how Aperol turned a 100-year-old regional aperitif into a global spritz phenomenon.

 
 
PHOTO: MARCO BERTORELLO/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

It’s orange, sparkling and everywhere. Campari’s Aperol has ignited sales of the spritz culture in the U.S. and cemented its brand as a hallmark of aspirational joie de vivre. But the journey to get there wasn’t so effortless. In this video, we break down the strategy behind Aperol’s rise—and the growing competition challenging its dominance.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING TODAY

• Economic data: The Labor Department releases July job openings.

 

• Earnings: Medtronic, Palo Alto Networks, Dell Technologies

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
$4.4 billion
 

The estimated cash payout that fast-fashion giant Shein would have owed early investors if it hadn’t sold shares by the end of the year. The company’s initial public offering in Hong Kong is allowing the retailer to convert $17.3 billion in preferred shares into ordinary equity—wiping that massive obligation off its books and avoiding a major drain on its balance sheet.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Londoners are stewing over supercar tourists who park wherever they want.

 

London’s luxury streets have a pesky problem: foreign supercars that park where they see fit, racking up tickets the drivers don’t pay. The city’s priciest neighborhoods become particularly clogged each summer as drivers escaping the Gulf’s scorching heat arrive with Ferraris, Lamborghinis and McLarens bearing Middle East license plates. The borough of Westminster, home to some of London’s toniest neighborhoods, said in a 2023 report that it sought to collect payment on 13,423 tickets issued to United Arab Emirates vehicles between 2018 and 2022. Only 1% paid.
